sections.title: The three jobs
sections.body: Concurrency tools solve different problems. WaitGroup tracks task completion. Mutex and atomic operations make shared-memory access safe. Channels and context coordinate communication, readiness, and cancellation. Selecting a tool begins by naming which of those jobs the program actually needs.

sections.title: The safety rule
sections.body: Concurrent access becomes a data race when conflicting operations on the same memory location are unordered by happens-before. A mutex unlock followed by a later lock, a matched channel send and receive, closing a channel and observing that close, atomics, and WaitGroup completion provide defined ordering. Timing delays and ordinary flags do not.

sections.title: Current Go details
sections.body: WaitGroup.Go, added in Go 1.25, starts and tracks a task and is preferred for that common case; its function must not panic. Add and Done remain valid when tasks are tracked manually. A Mutex and WaitGroup have useful zero values and must not be copied after first use. select chooses uniformly pseudo-randomly among communications that can proceed; nil cases are disabled, closed receives are ready, and default makes the operation non-blocking.

sections.title: Verification
sections.body: Run concurrent tests with go test -race and exercise realistic paths. The detector reports only races that occur during that execution, so a clean run is evidence, not proof. Keep cancellation ownership explicit, call returned CancelFuncs, and test that workers finish when consumers stop early.
